item.dc:creator: Micah Hanks
item.content:encoded:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

For as long as humans have watched the night sky, we have wondered about the moon , pondering everything from its alien appearance to its influence over phenomena on Earth such as ocean tides, climate stability, and even the natural rhythms of many organisms. Among the many questions we have about Earth's lone natural satellite, one remains preeminent: what are the moon's origins , and how long has it orbited Earth? Today, the leading theory among astronomers is that deep in our planet's past — perhaps within roughly the first 100 million years of solar system history — Earth collided with a planet-sized object, creating the moon within a period that may have been as short as just a few hours . Known as the giant-impact hypothesis, this proposed event involves a hypothetical Mars-sized protoplanet astronomers call Theia. The material ejected into orbit by the powerful impact in question would have accumulated afterward, forming the moon that we observe today. What do we know? Birth of a lunar origin hypothesis The evolution of this striking solution to one of the moon's most enduring mysteries goes back to 1946, when geologist Reginald Aldworth Daly was among the first to suggest that an impact event might explain the formation of the moon. Before Daly, scientists had been leaning toward theories that involved Earth's rapid spin billions of years ago, when each day may have at one time lasted as little as 2 or 3 hours . Decades later in the 1970s, researchers William Hartmann and Donald Davis developed their own models involving collisions of large bodies left over from planetary formation, which could collide with younger planets. Building on such ideas, other researchers went on to propose similar scenarios between the early Earth and a Mars-sized object. Early in the following decade, the concept eventually claimed its place as the leading lunar-formation process during a landmark conference held in Kona, Hawaii, in 1984. Earth's moon is thought to have formed when a Mars-sized object, called Theia, slammed into the proto-Earth more than 4.4 billion years ago, blasting out material that later coalesced into a large satellite as depicted in this artist's illustration. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Evidence of a planetary-scale collision The popularity of the giant-impact hypothesis can be attributed to the multiple lines of evidence supporting the impact scenario. For instance, researchers have long recognized the similar stable-isotope ratios between both moon rocks and those from Earth, strongly suggesting a link between their origins. Additionally, the unusually high angular momentum (or spin) of the Earth-moon system, when compared to observations of other rocky planets, also could be explained as one of the effects of a massive collision. Further clues can be found in the moon's composition, which reveals a relatively small iron core and lower density. This is significant to astronomers, since a hypothetical giant impact would have seen the suspected Theia protoplanet's metallic core merging with the young Earth's interior — meanwhile, lighter mantle and crust material from both worlds would have become dislodged and blasted into orbit, eventually helping form the moon. Another important piece of evidence involves the relative depletion of volatile substances (a chemical that easily turns into gas or vapor at room temperatures) in lunar material, which again suggests that it might have been lost during an extremely energetic event, an idea further supported by evidence that the early moon once possessed a substantial magma ocean. Illustration of the young Earth-Moon system. The Earth had recently formed when it was struck by a protoplanet, called Theia, roughly three times the size of Mars. Debris from the impact went into orbit where it quickly coalesced to form the Moon, probably within just a few thousand years. Initially the Earth and moon were much closer together than they are now, and spinning more quickly. In this depiction, debris from the collision continues to rain down on both worlds. (Image credit: Mark Garlick/Science Photo Library/Getty Images) What remains unknown? New research expands on the Theia hypothesis Still, several significant questions remain, including what precise conditions led to the impact, and how the resulting planetary material evolved into the moon as it appears today. Recently, a new study by Adeene Denton of Southwest Research Institute and colleagues at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory put a new spin on the Theia hypothesis, suggesting that the suspected ancient impact may have been significantly influenced by the heat and physical strength of the two colliding bodies. The team's findings challenge some long-held views about the giant-impact hypothesis, while lending new support to others. For instance, the team's simulations revealed that while some impacts lead to the creation of a disk of debris that later coalesces into a moon, under other conditions, simulations support the idea that the moon could have been formed in a remarkably short period of time — perhaps within around five hours . However, one of the primary issues with determining the exact conditions of the giant-impact hypothesis involves the ongoing debate over the moon's age. "There is a large controversy regarding the age of the moon," said Dr. Erik Asphaug, a planetary science professor at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and one of the new study's co-authors. Earth sets over the moon's curved limb in this photo captured by the Artemis II crew during their journey around the far side of the moon. (Image credit: NASA) In an email to Space, Asphaug explained some of the issues arising from this, since current estimates place the timing of the moon's formation anywhere from around 40 to 120 million years after the formation of the solar system. Therein lies part of the issue, according to Asphaug, who says this timing could have significant implications for models of the Theia impact. If it had been an earlier collision, Asphaug says this would have involved a hotter Theia due to the greater degree of radiogenic heating; by contrast, a later impact would have meant a cooler and stronger Theia. "I don't think we know enough yet to say the moon (and by corollary, the Earth) formed this way or that way," Asphaug told Space . "But knowing how temperature affects the result opens up a new dimension for viewing the problem, and that is always helpful because it shifts our frame of reference, like getting out of the car to have a walk around." A lunar enigma in time and space For researchers like Asphaug, understanding the moon's formation requires looking at it as more than just an event in space, but also as one in time. Doing so allows comparisons between three different metrics: isotopic decay, temperature-dependent material strength, and the geological record of debris striking other planets — a process through which he believes tighter constraints could be placed on precisely when the moon-forming impact might have occurred. Adeene Denton, the study's lead author, also emphasized the introduction of the time component her team's research brings to the table, telling Space in an email that the outcome of the moon-forming impact could have depended significantly on the timing of the collision. "Before, scientists have generally assumed that the outcome of the collision will be the same regardless of when it takes place," Denton wrote . "But now we know that temperature's effect on material properties, which is dictated by how old and/or cold the proto-Earth and Theia might be, alters things substantially." B

item.title: An Icon Reimagined: Maltina Unveils New Look And Same Nourishing Taste
item.description: Maltina , Nigeria’s pioneering malt brand, has unveiled a new visual identity. The new look celebrates 50 years of nourishment while preserving the trusted taste Nigerians know and love. The new identity presents Maltina through a more contemporary lens across its glass bottles, cans and PET bottles. The brand’s signature orange has been strengthened, while enhanced gold elements create a more distinctive and premium presence on the shelf. New design cues, including the gold crown cork, brighter sunrays, a more prominent golden barley icon, a bolder calcium coin and the “Since 1976” heritage mark, bring Maltina’s story of nourishment and heritage to life. The look may be new, but the nourishing Maltina consumers know and trust remains unchanged. Maltina is fortified with calcium, with one 33cl bottle providing the equivalent of half a glass of milk. The brand is also endorsed by the Nutrition Society of Nigeria as a non-alcoholic drink rich in Vitamin A. “ For 50 years, Maltina has grown alongside generations of Nigerians. This refreshed identity is an evolution of a much-loved brand, designed to keep Maltina fresh, relevant and connected to today’s consumers while preserving the nourishing taste they know and trust, ” said Sarah Agha , Marketing Director, Nigerian Breweries Plc . Rather than define the new look for consumers, Maltina is inviting Nigerians to share their own first impressions through the “ What’s Your Word? ” campaign. Across media, retail and consumer experiences, people will be encouraged to look again and describe the refreshed identity in one word. “This relaunch is about more than a new pack. It is an invitation for Nigerians to help shape the next chapter of a brand that has been part of their lives for five decades. We look forward to hearing the words the new Maltina inspires,” Agha added. Consumers will encounter the refreshed packs in stores, restaurants, bars and markets, supported by a nationwide media rollout, trade launches and immersive consumer activations designed to help Nigerians discover and experience the new look. The invitation is simple: experience the new Maltina and tell us what you see. What’s Your Word for the New Maltina? https://maltina.nbplc.com/ . About Maltina Maltina is a non-alcoholic malt drink from Nigerian Breweries Plc. For 50 years, the brand has been part of Nigerian homes and everyday moments, bringing together nourishment, happiness and shared experiences across generations. item.title: Ayra Starr Is Taking Her Starrgirl World Tour to Europe and North America in 2027
item.description: Ayra Starr is set to bring her hit singles to the NFL London Game halftime show on 11th October Ladies and gentlemen, we reckon that cities in Europe, the UK and North America will come alive in purple from January 2027 to April 2027 because the Starrgirl herself, Ayra Starr , has officially announced her grand return to global stages. If you have been keeping up with global music headlines, you already know Oyinkansola Sarah Aderibigbe —famously known across the world as Ayra Starr—is in a league of her own. She recently made history as the very first African artiste to headline an NFL halftime show during the 2026 International Games fixture in London, treating a packed stadium crowd to a performance that cemented Afrobeats on one of sport’s biggest entertainment platforms. Fresh off that landmark milestone and the release of her third studio album, Starrgirl, the Mavin global sensation is packing her bags to take the project on a massive multi-continent run. Ayra Starr performing at the NFL Halftime Show in London The upcoming Starrgirl World Tour kicks off its main international leg on 20 January 2027 in Cologne, Germany. From there, Ayra heads to Amsterdam on 21 January, Paris on 24 January, Milan on 27 January, Zurich on 29 January, and Brussels on 31 January. Her UK lovers get their turn on 2 February 2027, when she steps onto the London stage for a night that promises to be an absolute highlight of the winter season. North American fans pick up the excitement starting 18 March 2027 in Houston, Texas. The road trip continues across Dallas, Atlanta, Silver Spring, Boston, Philadelphia, Brooklyn, Chicago, Minneapolis, Denver, and San Francisco, alongside Canadian stops in Toronto and Montreal through early April. item.title: Broadcom Wi-Fi bug turns sweet 16, still lets strangers hijack your router
item.description: A 16-year-old security flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi software could let attackers hijack millions of routers without knowing the network password, even though the chipmaker reportedly knew about the problem since 2018. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the vulnerability , dubbed "WPSplinter," revealing two bugs in Broadcom's proprietary Wi-Fi implementation that date back to at least 2010. An attempted fix arrived eight years later, but Kaiser claims it didn't fully resolve the problem. The bugs lie in Broadcom's handling of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets users connect devices to a wireless network without manually entering a password. Kaiser found that specially crafted WPS messages could corrupt the router's memory, allowing someone within Wi-Fi range to run their own code on the device. They wouldn't need the Wi-Fi password, and the router's owner wouldn't have to do a thing. Kaiser demonstrated working exploits against routers supplied by Belgian internet providers Proximus and Orange. In one attack against an ASKEY TCG3000 gateway, he ran code on the device, pulled its Wi-Fi password from memory, and sent it back over the air. He then used the stolen credentials to join the network. He also found the flaw in Netgear and Technicolor routers supplied by VOO. He estimates that around 850,000 Proximus gateways could be affected, along with 500,000 at VOO and 210,000 at Orange Belgium. That puts the potential total at 1.56 million routers in Belgium alone, although Kaiser admits the figures are rough estimates. However, the problem is unlikely to stop at the Belgian border. Broadcom's Wi-Fi technology is used by dozens of manufacturers across hundreds of products, meaning the number of affected devices worldwide could be considerably higher. According to Kaiser, the chipmaker knew about the vulnerability back in 2018 and released a partial fix without publicly disclosing the problem. It subsequently recommended that manufacturers move away from its proprietary implementation and use the open-source hostapd software instead. Owners of routers running Broadcom's older eCos-based chips, including the BCM3380, BCM3383, and BCM33834, are in a particularly grim position. Kaiser calls the flaw a "forever day," meaning those devices may never get a fix. Routers using Linux-based BCM3390, BCM65xx, and BCM68xx chips aren't necessarily off the hook either, unless their manufacturers switch to hostapd. That leaves some older routers with no obvious route to a fix, while others depend on their manufacturers updating software that may be years out of support. Kaiser first reported the vulnerabilities to Broadcom on July 18, followed by a second report on July 27, giving the company and affected vendors 90 days before public disclosure. Broadcom responded on July 28 to say a patch was available and advised him to contact affected manufacturers directly. The following day, however, the company declined to assign a CVE identifier or prov

item.content:encoded: A 16-year-old security flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi software could let attackers hijack millions of routers without knowing the network password, even though the chipmaker reportedly knew about the problem since 2018. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the vulnerability , dubbed "WPSplinter," revealing two bugs in Broadcom's proprietary Wi-Fi implementation that date back to at least 2010. An attempted fix arrived eight years later, but Kaiser claims it didn't fully resolve the problem. The bugs lie in Broadcom's handling of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets users connect devices to a wireless network without manually entering a password. Kaiser found that specially crafted WPS messages could corrupt the router's memory, allowing someone within Wi-Fi range to run their own code on the device. They wouldn't need the Wi-Fi password, and the router's owner wouldn't have to do a thing. Kaiser demonstrated working exploits against routers supplied by Belgian internet providers Proximus and Orange. In one attack against an ASKEY TCG3000 gateway, he ran code on the device, pulled its Wi-Fi password from memory, and sent it back over the air. He then used the stolen credentials to join the network. He also found the flaw in Netgear and Technicolor routers supplied by VOO. He estimates that around 850,000 Proximus gateways could be affected, along with 500,000 at VOO and 210,000 at Orange Belgium. That puts the potential total at 1.56 million routers in Belgium alone, although Kaiser admits the figures are rough estimates. However, the problem is unlikely to stop at the Belgian border. Broadcom's Wi-Fi technology is used by dozens of manufacturers across hundreds of products, meaning the number of affected devices worldwide could be considerably higher. According to Kaiser, the chipmaker knew about the vulnerability back in 2018 and released a partial fix without publicly disclosing the problem. It subsequently recommended that manufacturers move away from its proprietary implementation and use the open-source hostapd software instead. Owners of routers running Broadcom's older eCos-based chips, including the BCM3380, BCM3383, and BCM33834, are in a particularly grim position. Kaiser calls the flaw a "forever day," meaning those devices may never get a fix. Routers using Linux-based BCM3390, BCM65xx, and BCM68xx chips aren't necessarily off the hook either, unless their manufacturers switch to hostapd. That leaves some older routers with no obvious route to a fix, while others depend on their manufacturers updating software that may be years out of support. Kaiser first reported the vulnerabilities to Broadcom on July 18, followed by a second report on July 27, giving the company and affected vendors 90 days before public disclosure. Broadcom responded on July 28 to say a patch was available and advised him to contact affected manufacturers directly. The following day, however, the company declined to assign a CVE identifier or provide him with a copy of the notification it said it had sent to manufacturers through its customer portal. Kaiser also contacted Proximus, attempted to reach Orange Belgium and VOO, and passed his findings to Belgium's national cybersecurity authorities. He subsequently opened a case with CERT/CC, which closed it on August 4 because Broadcom was itself a CVE Numbering Authority and had declined to register the vulnerability. By October 15, a day before his presentation, Kaiser said none of the affected devices he had identified had received a patch. Kaiser hasn't reported evidence of attacks in the wild, but the potential for mischief is considerable. Someone parked outside a home or office could potentially compromise a vulnerable router, steal network credentials, or use their access to interfere with traffic. Kaiser also credited AI with speeding up the investigation. He reckons the work would ordinarily have taken him months, but with the help of frontier models, he finished it in less than a week. ®

item.title: Seven Women, Seven Innovations: InnovateNaija’s Role in Nigeria’s Tech Story
item.description: Through the NASENI and AfriLabs-backed InnovateNaija Challenge, seven women brought bold technological ideas to the national stage, and one of them took home the ultimate prize. Their journey shows what is possible when Nigerian women are given the platform, support, and opportunity to build. For years, conversations about Nigeria’s technology ecosystem have centred on the scale of the industry, the growth of startups, and the young people building the next generation of solutions. But there is another part of that story that deserves greater attention: the women building too. Seven women were among the 15 finalists of the InnovateNaija Challenge , a national technology and innovation competition led by the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure ( NASENI ), in partnership with AfriLabs and the Federal Ministry of Youth Development. Coming from different parts of the country and working across diverse fields, these women built solutions that go far beyond the idea of simply participating in technology. They designed, engineered, and developed products responding to real problems in healthcare, agriculture, energy, environmental sustainability, and everyday life. A Historic Victory for Agricultural Hardware The national pitch event, held October 6, 2026 , saw all 15 finalists present physical prototypes before industry experts, global investors, and policymakers. Emerging as the overall grand prize winner of ₦100 million was Abia State innovator Adaeze Ruth Akpagbula , co-founder of Farm Speak , for her PenKeep Smart Poultry Climate Control System . Designed to help farmers manage climate-related challenges across poultry, aquaculture, greenhouse, and smart irrigation systems, PenKeep demonstrates how deep tech can be applied to fundamental agricultural challenges. For Akpagbula, who identified funding, infrastructure, and electricity as major hurdles for hardware innovators in Nigeria, the ₦100 million award will help expand her company’s production capacity and enable the technology to reach more farmers. Innovating Across Every Sector Akpagbula’s top finish was part of a larger showing by female innovators across the competition. Among the seven female finalists was Kemisola Bolarinwa from Ekiti State, whose innovation, the Smart Bra Cup Diagnostic Device , explores the use of technology in breast health. Her work demonstrates how engineering can be directly applied to healthcare challenges that have historically received limited attention. The women of InnovateNaija tackled broad issues across multiple sectors. Elizabeth Chioma Chiketarauba of Imo State developed Torquenova , an electric vehicle and main power generator that can be recharged using an in-built solar-powered system or mains supply, bringing together mobility, energy, and renewable technology. Rita Idehai of Edo State developed an Automated Reverse Vending Machine, applying technology to waste management and environmental sustainability. Chinyere Esther Onwumel

For Akpagbula, who identified funding, infrastructure, and electricity as major hurdles for hardware innovators in Nigeria, the ₦100 million award will help expand her company’s production capacity and enable the technology to reach more farmers. Innovating Across Every Sector Akpagbula’s top finish was part of a larger showing by female innovators across the competition. Among the seven female finalists was Kemisola Bolarinwa from Ekiti State, whose innovation, the Smart Bra Cup Diagnostic Device , explores the use of technology in breast health. Her work demonstrates how engineering can be directly applied to healthcare challenges that have historically received limited attention. The women of InnovateNaija tackled broad issues across multiple sectors. Elizabeth Chioma Chiketarauba of Imo State developed Torquenova , an electric vehicle and main power generator that can be recharged using an in-built solar-powered system or mains supply, bringing together mobility, energy, and renewable technology. Rita Idehai of Edo State developed an Automated Reverse Vending Machine, applying technology to waste management and environmental sustainability. Chinyere Esther Onwumelu of Nasarawa State created a Gas-Level Monitoring and Community Gas Metering System , addressing energy access and accountability. Khadija Adamu Dandad a of Kano State developed the Shepall App , demonstrating the role digital solutions can play in addressing practical everyday needs. Miriam Ashiemar Agbo of Benue State created the Anatsor Integrated Poultry Management System , applying technology to agricultural productivity and livestock management. And Adaeze Ruth Akpagbula of Abia State developed PenKeep , advancing smart poultry climate control and ultimately earning the top spot on the national stage. A Technology Story That Includes Women Their stories matter far beyond the competition itself. Nigeria’s technology sector needs innovators who can identify problems, build solutions, and take concepts from an idea to a tangible product. The presence and eventual victory of female innovators among the InnovateNaija finalists provides a clear reminder that Nigerian women are already contributing to high-impact innovation. These finalists are engineers, inventors, developers, and problem-solvers. Their innovations span different sectors, states, and use cases. What connects them is not simply the problems they are solving, but the fact that they are building solutions themselves. Creating Room for the Next Generation of Women Builders Platforms such as InnovateNaija play an important role in creating more room for this kind of innovation. Led by NASENI alongside AfriLabs and the Federal Ministry of Youth Development, the challenge gave grassroots innovators a national stage to showcase their work and access opportunities for funding, technical expertise, manufacturing support, and scale. Beyond the cash prizes, which included a ₦100 million grand prize alongside ₦30 million and ₦20 million grants for the runners-up, all 15 finalists gained long-term access to advanced manufacturing tools and infrastructure across NASENI’s nationwide technology institutes. Most importantly, Adaeze Akpagbula’s victory and the work of her fellow female finalists give young Nigerian girls something tangible to see. A student with an idea can look at InnovateNaija and see that she does not have to wait for someone else to build the future. She can build it herself, and she can win. You're probably familiar with some of Voyager's iconic images, like the Pale Blue Dot and and its portraits of the outer planets. Those photos and observations wouldn't have been possible without Voyager's imaging team, eight members of which were selected from scientists from around the world. The UK's sole representative, Dr. Garry Hunt, joins us on this episode of The Kettle to discuss his role in the Voyager program, the future of the mission, and the state of science in the UK, US, and beyond. With us to talk about this is Reg Reporter Richard Speed and our very special guest, British astrophysicist Dr. Garry Hunt who was a member of the original Voyager imaging team. Thank you so much, Dr. Hunt, for coming on. item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: It's been nearly half a century since the Voyager probes launched from Earth on a mission to explore the outer solar system, and they're still running. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle on this page, Spotify , Apple Podcasts , or YouTube . You can also subscribe on those platforms to be notified when a new episode goes live. You're probably familiar with some of Voyager's iconic images, like the Pale Blue Dot and and its portraits of the outer planets. The UK's sole representative, Dr. Garry Hunt, joins us on this episode of The Kettle to discuss his role in the Voyager program, the future of the mission, and the state of science in the UK, US, and beyond. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:01) Hi everyone, and welcome to another episode of The Register ’s Kettle Podcast. I'm your host, Brandon Vigliarolo, and we have a very special episode for you this week. We're gonna step away from the doom and gloom of AI and the silliness of Silicon Valley to talk about something and to someone of considerably more historic importance. The Voyager space missions will mark fifty years of exploring the solar system and beyond next year. With us to talk about this is Reg Reporter Richard Speed and our very special guest, British astrophysicist Dr. Garry Hunt who was a member of the original Voyager imaging team. Thank you so much, Dr. Hunt, for coming on. And I'm gonna turn this over to Richard today, since you two have such a history together working on stories for The Reg , and I'm excited to hear about what he's going to pick your brain about. So Richard, take it away. Richard Speed (00:46) Well Dr. Hunt, we've spoken a lot about the Voyager project over the years, but for anyone who's not aware of it, I wonder if you could summarize the mission, which is, I know, a big ask, and also what your role in it is and was. Garry Hunt (01:00) Well indeed, it's a unique mission in the sense that every 176 years the major planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, line up virtually in a straight line. And we wanted to explore the outer planets 'cause we've never been there before. I'm talking in the 1970s, late 1960s, '70s. So this is an unknown world. We thought that the major planets were keys to understanding the origin of the solar system, indeed the origin of life, so sending space missions there was a priority. But it needed to be done in a very economical way. With the planets lined up, that meant we could get there in the quickest way, requiring less fuel, and it would be the best way of going about it. So the opportunity came and NASA funded a mission to send two spacecraft at this unique time, which was in the mid '70s, 1977, to the major planets. NASA sent out an invitation to tender. They selected the ten instruments. Imaging had as an instrument in concept had been suggested, but they wanted a team of real scientists, not astronomers, not basic astronomers. They understood this is a chance to do real detailed science, real physics, real chemistry, the whole understanding of what went on. So they were looking for an interdisciplinary group of people. They selected eight people from invitations and I gather there were about nearly a thousand people proposed and of those eight I was chosen. Brandon (02:43) Wow. Garry Hunt (02:44) So I decided I suddenly found myself in this incredible position. I'm there to represent atmospheric physics. I want to understand the physics, the meteorology of the major planets. So here is an opportunity to explore the outer planets to learn about why we wanted to go to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. However, funding was tight. The president at the time was Nixon, and we only had funding as far as Jupiter and Saturn. So we were treading new territory. At the time the mission was sort of decided, we had not been through the asteroid belt. So the first question was: would the spacecraft even get that far? And of course the Pioneers had just been launched at the beginning of the '70s and they managed to get through and raised a lot of questions. So I was part of the imaging team, this amazing set of what I will call prima donnas, because we all were. They were from Carl Sagan to Vern Suomi, who was a meteorologist, to Brad Smith, a whole collection of people. And we had to design the imaging system, the cameras, and be part of the organization that developed the choice of trajectories and all the other facets of this mission. In other words, we had to understand the risks as well as the potential rewards that came from it. So it was a big responsibility. And to put the whole thing in real context, I learnt in December '72 from NASA that I'd been selected. We had our first mission meetings in February of '73, and we had until the summer of 1977 to get the spacecraft launched. And the window for launching was ten days. So this was really a big precision job. So large responsibility and had many opportunities, not only to do the science, but the work that I was doing when I took the data back to the UK was to actually serve as a trigger for planetary research within the UK. So this really was a major major part of a new world, new understanding. And as we have learned over the years, we have made history and just about all the observations we've made. Richard Speed (05:16) Okay, great, thank you. So, I mean, as you said, it's been coming out for half a century, 50 years since the spacecraft were launched on their mission and they've been, as you say, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and so on. I was just wondering, why do you think they've lasted for so long? Because it's just incredible, really if you think about it. Garry Hunt (05:36) Well, firstly I will put my hand up and say that the engineers of JPL are exceptional. We've had a few hitches and they've overcome it. First of all, we also said we want a spacecraft. It's going to unknown territories. We don't know how long it's going to last. Reliability was the key. So it was built around the Mariners, which have been the bedrock of the earlier missions to around Mars and flying by Venus. So that was the first thing. And so many of the aspects of it were built from equipment from the mid-sixties. So the issue is even more exciting to think that here we are 50 years after launch flying a spacecraft with equipment which was already 10 years old by the time we got it there. So this really is an example of reliability, which is the bottleneck. And of course, the other aspect of it we built in redundancy as well. So we knew that, if things went wrong, we had to find a way of easily overcoming it. As it's drifting away at the speed of thirty thousand miles an hour, you can't just sort of go out and repair it. You've got to be able to do things while the spacecraft is in motion. So there's a certain amount of redundancy, built in reliability, incredibly good careful planning, absolutely brilliant engineers who to this day are doing the most incredible things. Richard Speed (07:05) Well, yes, I have to say, I agree, having spoken to the current Voyager team, they are a bunch of very impressive individuals. And they seem to keep eking out more and more life from the spacecraft. I know it's powered by RTGs, which will eventually expire and there won't be enough power to keep it going. But it seems they'll be able to continue well into the 2030s, maybe even beyond. I mean, what do you think is going to end the mission because I mean it must be coming up. Do you think it'll be a hardware failure? We have had some spacecraft failures over the years or do you think it's going to be more prosaic? Perhaps it'll be just a lack of funding. Garry Hunt (07:41) Well, if you go back to our elementary school physics, we know that as it moves away the signal strength di

item.title: 5 New Music Videos You Need to Watch This Week: Victony, Tyla, Phyno & More
item.description: Nigerian singer-songwriter Victony wearing a glossy leather outfit on set during the production of the SLICK Remix, featuring American stars Don Toliver and Summer Walker, off his sophomore album STARLIFE. A new week calls for fresh music, and there’s plenty to add to your watchlist. From Victony bringing Don Toliver and Summer Walker into the mix for the “ SLICK ” remix to Tyla ’s dance-ready “ That Girl ” and Phyno ’s romantic “Beautiful”, there’s something for every mood. We’re also looking back at Ayra Starr ’s performance at the 2026 NFL international halftime show and making room for Anendlessocean ’s reflective “ Promises ”. Here are five music releases and performances to check out this week. Victony: “SLICK (Remix)” ft. Don Toliver & Summer Walker Victony has given “SLICK” a new twist, and this time, he’s brought Don Toliver and Summer Walker along for the ride. The original track appears on his sophomore album, STARLIFE, while the remix introduces a fresh mix of R&B vocals and melodies. With three artistes bringing their different sounds to the same record, there’s plenty to enjoy here. Tyla: “That Girl” If you’re looking for something to get you moving, Tyla has you covered with “That Girl” from her project A*Pop. The song draws on South Africa’s popular Phara Walk dance culture, pairing catchy rhythms with Tyla’s smooth vocals. It’s playful, danceable and one you might find yourself returning to throughout the week. Anendlessocean: “Promises” Anendlessocean offers a place for reflection, gratitude and rest with “Promises”. Rooted in faith and the assurance that God will come through again, the song invites listeners to pause, reflect and find comfort in the belief that He will do it again. It’s one to turn to when you need a little reminder to trust the journey. Phyno: “Beautiful” Ezege is back with “Beautiful”, a love letter to the woman who makes everything make sense. Smooth, heartfelt and unmistakably Phyno, the track blends Igbo, Pidgin and English over a melody made for the ones you hold close. Taken from his project Let That Sink In (LTSI), the song celebrates love in a way that feels personal and familiar. The official music video features actress and media personality Nancy Isime, giving the romantic track a visual companion. Ayra Starr: 2026 NFL Halftime Performance Ayra Starr took Afrobeats to the NFL international stage on 11 October, headlining the halftime show during the Philadelphia Eagles vs Jacksonville Jaguars game at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London. She opened her set with “Heaven Baby”, her collaboration with ZAYN, before performing “Santa”, “Rush” and “Dangerous”, and closing with a medley of “Hot Body” and “Ms. Paper”. The performance marked a major milestone for the Nigerian star, who became the first African artiste to headline an NFL International Games halftime show. The song draws on South Africa’s popular Phara Walk dance culture, pairing catchy rhythms with Tyla’s smooth vocals. It’s playful, danceable and one you might find yourself returning to throughout the week. Anendlessocean: “Promises” Anendlessocean offers a place for reflection, gratitude and rest with “Promises”. Rooted in faith and the assurance that God will come through again, the song invites listeners to pause, reflect and find comfort in the belief that He will do it again. It’s one to turn to when you need a little reminder to trust the journey. Phyno: “Beautiful” Ezege is back with “Beautiful”, a love letter to the woman who makes everything make sense. Smooth, heartfelt and unmistakably Phyno, the track blends Igbo, Pidgin and English over a melody made for the ones you hold close. Taken from his project Let That Sink In (LTSI), the song celebrates love in a way that feels personal and familiar. The official music video features actress and media personality Nancy Isime, giving the romantic track a visual companion. Ayra Starr: 2026 NFL Halftime Performance Ayra Starr took Afrobeats to the NFL international stage on 11 October, headlining the halftime show during the Philadelphia Eagles vs Jacksonville Jaguars game at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London. She opened her set with “Heaven Baby”, her collaboration with ZAYN, before performing “Santa”, “Rush” and “Dangerous”, and closing with a medley of “Hot Body” and “Ms. Paper”. The performance marked a major milestone for the Nigerian star, who became the first African artiste to headline an NFL International Games halftime show. The post 5 New Music Videos You Need to Watch This Week: Victony, Tyla, Phyno & More appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Museum exhibit reveals the intricate workings of a knackered Dell
item.description: Today's entry in the catalog of bork comes from Coventry's Herbert Art Gallery & Museum, where an information terminal is showing more about the hardware behind the scenes than the objects on display. Register reader Jeffrey Borinsky spotted the panel, which should have demonstrated a Jacquard loom in action but was instead displaying a warning about its host PC's failing battery. The Jacquard loom was a clever device dating back to the dawn of the 19th century. It used punched cards to control a loom's weaving patterns. The result was complicated and repeatable textile designs that reduced the need for skilled humans. Register readers of a certain age are doubtless nodding sagely at the mention of punched cards, which would go on to become foundational in the world of computing. Borinsky reported that several screens at the museum were in distress. Ribbon weaving was Coventry's main industry from the early 1700s until the 1860s, so a demonstration of Jacquard weaving fits right in, even if the bleating about the BIOS battery was probably not what Joseph Jacquard had in mind. The device running behind the scenes is a Dell OptiPlex 755, likely from around 2007. Not quite centuries old like a Jacquard loom, but certainly getting on a bit in the IT world. The first iPhone arrived in 2007, and a PC of a similar vintage likely shipped with Windows XP or Windows Vista. The CMOS battery is on the way out. Dell specifies a CR2032 coin cell, so replacement should be straightforward after disconnecting the power and taking anti-static precautions. Rather less traumatic than the head-in-hands moment when a retro enthusiast discovers a leaking battery has eaten through delicate circuit traces. A fresh battery and restored BIOS settings should be enough to get the loom demonstration weaving again. Given how important punched cards became in the history of computing, we'd recommend visiting anywhere that shows how a Jacquard loom operated. At least it didn't need a battery-backed BIOS to do its thing. ®

item.description: Exclusive: Using test accounts acting as 13-year-olds, Tech Transparency Project downloaded 135 apps with features to generate nonconsensual nude imagery In December 2025, Morgan Dorfman received distressing news: a student at her daughter’s Pennsylvania high school was making AI-generated pornographic material using the daughter’s image. He was using an artificial intelligence image-editing app called Movely to create sexual videos from pictures of her daughter and five other girls. Continue reading...

item.title: Watch Japan launch a bold sample-return mission to Mars moon Phobos today
item.description: null Editor's note: Japan launched its bold MMX sample-return mission to the Mars moon Phobos on Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT). Watch a replay of the liftoff and read our launch story here. Japan will launch an epic mission to Mars today (Oct. 19), and you can watch the action live. The Martian Moons eXploration ( MMX ) mission is scheduled to lift off atop an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center today at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. on Oct. 20 local Japan time). You can watch it live via the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Coverage will begin at 2:45 p.m. EDT (1845 GMT). An artist’s concept of JAXA’s MMX spacecraft during its Mars orbit insertion. The Martian moon Phobos, which MMX will explore and sample, is in the background. (Image credit: JAXA) As its full name suggests, MMX will focus on Mars ' two moons, Phobos and Deimos . They're both tiny compared to Earth's own moon; Phobos is just 14 miles (22 kilometers) wide, and Deimos is even smaller, with a diameter of about 8 miles (13 km). They're also quite mysterious. While astronomers have a pretty clear understanding of our own moon's birth — it coalesced from material blasted into space when a Mars-sized planet slammed into Earth long ago — there's no consensus about Phobos and Deimos' origin story. The duo "may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars' gravity billions of years ago," Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters, said in an Oct. 15 statement . (NASA is a partner on the mission, providing a scientific instrument, a technology demonstration, communication support and funding for American scientists on the MMX team.) "Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds," Statler added. MMX will help provide that answer, if all goes according to plan. The spacecraft will arrive in the Mars system in August 2027, then slip into orbit around Phobos a month later. It will study that moon and Deimos from a distance for about 18 months, then deploy the French-German Idefix rover onto Phobos' surface in early 2029. The 55-pound (25 kilograms) Idefix "has two main tasks: providing information to prepare for the landing of the main spacecraft to collect samples, and analyzing the composition and texture of Phobos' surface," European Space Agency officials wrote in an MMX mission description . "The gravity on Phobos is so low that Idefix will only weigh the equivalent of 15 grams [0.5 ounces] on its surface!" they added. The MMX mothership's Phobos landing will occur in 2030. The spacecraft will grab at least 10 grams (0.4 ounces) of samples from the moon, then head back toward Earth with this extraterrestrial bounty. The Martian moon Phobos, which MMX will explore and sample, is in the background. (Image credit: JAXA) As its full name suggests, MMX will focus on Mars ' two moons, Phobos and Deimos . (NASA is a partner on the mission, providing a scientific instrument, a technology demonstration, communication support and funding for American scientists on the MMX team.) "Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds," Statler added. MMX will help provide that answer, if all goes according to plan. The spacecraft will arrive in the Mars system in August 2027, then slip into orbit around Phobos a month later. It will study that moon and Deimos from a distance for about 18 months, then deploy the French-German Idefix rover onto Phobos' surface in early 2029. The 55-pound (25 kilograms) Idefix "has two main tasks: providing information to prepare for the landing of the main spacecraft to collect samples, and analyzing the composition and texture of Phobos' surface," European Space Agency officials wrote in an MMX mission description . "The gravity on Phobos is so low that Idefix will only weigh the equivalent of 15 grams [0.5 ounces] on its surface!" they added. The MMX mothership's Phobos landing will occur in 2030. The spacecraft will grab at least 10 grams (0.4 ounces) of samples from the moon, then head back toward Earth with this extraterrestrial bounty. MMX's return capsule will land here in 2031, after which scientists around the world will scrutinize the Phobos sample for clues about the history and evolution of Mars and our solar system more broadly. Engineers conduct a thermal vacuum test with JAXA's MMX Mars moon sample-return spacecraft. JAXA posted this image on X on May 15, 2025. (Image credit: JAXA) MMX was originally supposed to launch in 2024, but issues with the H3 rocket prevented it from doing so. Mars and Earth align properly for interplanetary launches just once every 26 months, so MMX had to wait a while for its next chance. Japan already has an impressive sample-return track record. The country's Hayabusa mission brought home pieces of the asteroid Itokawa in 2010, for example, and Hayabusa2 did the same with material from the space rock Ryugu a decade later.

item.title: Microsoft’s second-hand licensing appeal gets the brush-off
item.description: Microsoft has failed to win permission to appeal to the UK Supreme Court in the long-running legal spat with ValueLicensing after the Court of Appeal refused its application. The US megacorp was challenging a November 2025 ruling in ValueLicensing's favor that VL may resell pre-owned software licenses. That judgment was unambiguous, but Microsoft told The Register at the time that it would seek permission to appeal. That request was rejected last week in blunt terms. No reasons were given for the refusal, just the words "It is ordered that the application is refused." It isn't quite the end of the road. Microsoft could apply to the Supreme Court itself, but it would need to file within 28 days and show a compelling reason why the Court of Appeal was wrong to refuse its appeal. Things are looking dicey for Microsoft in the case that started in 2021 when ValueLicensing sued Microsoft for £270 million over claims that the Windows maker choked off the supply of surplus Office licenses. Microsoft denied any wrongdoing and Instead attempted to reframe the case as a copyright dispute. The UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal rejected Microsoft's arguments and a subsequent appeal. A recently published Consent Order adds to the pressure. It demands documents from past and present Microsoft bosses, including a potentially explosive internal deck titled "Second-Hand Software Presentation" (SHS). The contents of the file are unknown, but the Consent Order refers to it as a "Known Adverse Document." It dates back to 2013, a few years after Office 365 was launched. The order also asks why Microsoft waited until the end of 2025 to disclose the document’s existence, a few years after Office 365 launched. To add a little more spice, Alexander Wolfson is listed as an intervener on the appeal refusal. He is the proposed class representative in a separate claim filed on behalf of millions of UK customers seeking between £1.3 billion to £3.5 billion in compensation from Microsoft over its conduct regarding pre-owned licenses. ValueLicensing and Microsoft declined to comment on the latest development. Appeals aside, the next stage will be a Witness Statement from Microsoft explaining who knew what and when, followed by further disclosure. ®

item.title: AI’s epic cash call is matched only by its ability to strangle revenue streams
item.description: As it was written , so it has come to pass. A while back, we suggested that given how good AI was at code analysis, it would become possible to clone large applications. And then where would we be? Here, that’s where. An industrious individual has released source code and binaries for Claude-copied Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative Suite programs, disappointingly not calling elements of the latter Fauxtoshop . They’re in pre-alpha states of incomplete bugginess, but with substantial functionality, which is proof of how insanely productive AI can be given a task needing zero creativity and wearing "This is what a proof of concept looks like" and "Unintended Consquesences" T-shirts. They could also add Karma Police to their wardrobe. It’s clear that Microsoft and Adobe are facing some competition from what their rival describes as "clean-room reimplementations." It’s also unclear that there is any law against it. You can’t copyright functionality, the code has been generated in Rust with claimed clean-room conditions, and while there may be something in claiming that the works are substantially derivative, there’s a big problem here. Companies that sell AI trained on the biggest theft of IP in history are going to need unmatched legal dexterity to claim that AI shouldn’t be allowed to sully their own IP. Chutzpah used to be defined as a child on trial for murdering their parents begging for mercy on the grounds that they’re an orphan. We’ll have to update that. The post-codeclone world is going to be interesting. Everything becomes effectively open source, which closes down substantial revenue streams for big companies who had assumed lock-in. The motivation to build ab-initio alternatives may go away, in open source as well as closed. The push to subscription-only cloud-hosted products, where nobody can get their thieving AI prompts on binaries, seems an obvious counter move, but AI can control and scrape a web interface, which is all it needs. It's an arms race that won’t be won by humans. Code cloning is just the latest case of AI being so disruptive it threatens its creators. Another is the doom loop that Microsoft-OpenAI acknowledged in internal emails : by siphoning away the ad revenue that pays for content, AI chokes off the data it depends on. It's deforestation by companies that built their business on other people's IP. The biggest potential point of failure is the money. How revenues will hold up against cheaper or free Chinese models is a concern, given the high importance assigned by Beijing to develop AI as a global influence vector. The models themselves are very efficient, in part because of export regulations on high-end silicon and something of a glut of older datacenters. This wouldn’t be the first time restricting access to technology is an evolutionary driver with a poor outcome for those doing the restricting. item.dc:creator: Rupert Goodwins
item.content:encoded: As it was written , so it has come to pass. A while back, we suggested that given how good AI was at code analysis, it would become possible to clone large applications. And then where would we be? Here, that’s where. An industrious individual has released source code and binaries for Claude-copied Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative Suite programs, disappointingly not calling elements of the latter Fauxtoshop . They’re in pre-alpha states of incomplete bugginess, but with substantial functionality, which is proof of how insanely productive AI can be given a task needing zero creativity and wearing "This is what a proof of concept looks like" and "Unintended Consquesences" T-shirts. They could also add Karma Police to their wardrobe. It’s clear that Microsoft and Adobe are facing some competition from what their rival describes as "clean-room reimplementations." It’s also unclear that there is any law against it. You can’t copyright functionality, the code has been generated in Rust with claimed clean-room conditions, and while there may be something in claiming that the works are substantially derivative, there’s a big problem here. Companies that sell AI trained on the biggest theft of IP in history are going to need unmatched legal dexterity to claim that AI shouldn’t be allowed to sully their own IP. Chutzpah used to be defined as a child on trial for murdering their parents begging for mercy on the grounds that they’re an orphan. We’ll have to update that. The post-codeclone world is going to be interesting. Everything becomes effectively open source, which closes down substantial revenue streams for big companies who had assumed lock-in. The motivation to build ab-initio alternatives may go away, in open source as well as closed. The push to subscription-only cloud-hosted products, where nobody can get their thieving AI prompts on binaries, seems an obvious counter move, but AI can control and scrape a web interface, which is all it needs. It's an arms race that won’t be won by humans. Code cloning is just the latest case of AI being so disruptive it threatens its creators. Another is the doom loop that Microsoft-OpenAI acknowledged in internal emails : by siphoning away the ad revenue that pays for content, AI chokes off the data it depends on. It's deforestation by companies that built their business on other people's IP. The biggest potential point of failure is the money. How revenues will hold up against cheaper or free Chinese models is a concern, given the high importance assigned by Beijing to develop AI as a global influence vector. The models themselves are very efficient, in part because of export regulations on high-end silicon and something of a glut of older datacenters. This wouldn’t be the first time restricting access to technology is an evolutionary driver with a poor outcome for those doing the restricting. A much bigger issue is: where will the money come from to build the infrastructure that is needed to support the claims AI is using to justify its growth. Gartner says that there’s not enough return on investment to drive that growth, while a much more engaging SemiAnalysis podcast predicts total capex by 2030 of $11 trillion and asks where it’s going to come from. If you’re interested in understanding AI and aren't following SemiAnalysis, you’re not interested in understanding AI, and while the outfit is relentlessly optimistic it’s also wildly well-informed. In this case, the structure of the investment market for AI is picked apart. It is very weird. Neocloud is made up of startups with a voracious appetite for cash, but no investment grade status . Thus, Nvidia backstops them, guaranteeing to rent unsold capacity for a fixed price for long enough to guarantee enough revenue to attract other investment. Other cash-rich big tech companies do similar things. This backstopping, also known more wryly as "balance sheet as a service," effectively shifts more risk to investment-rated companies. It's an increasingly important capex enabler, but as SemiAnalysis says, it’s necessarily limited, especially if AI itself has blown a hole in the enterprise. Or take the residual value of the older compute. Normally, the book value and revenue capabilities of datacenter chips depreciates over five years or so to some nominal value. That’s not happening here, where chips of that vintage are suddenly producing the same or more revenue than they did when they were new. Such are the peculiarities of a supply-constrained market used to rapid obsolescence. Surely a good thing, though? No. It’s another strange and hard-to-model factor in a market defined by strange and hard-to-model factors. Don’t even mention AGI. Or models too dangerous to use. Or model collapse. Many investors do not like the strange and hard to model, including huge pools of institutional funds. There are models that can blend in risk-averse investors to speculative investments, but those who remember the clever models that blew up the global economy nearly twenty years ago are not yet all dead. The tl;dr of the answer to where do you get enough money to make AI work as promised, is: nobody knows. What happens if the capex has no cap to ex? See previous answer. It may be an infantile affliction to have animation clips come to mind when considering AI, but it can’t be helped. Agentic AI? Mickey Mouse as the sorcerer's apprentice in Fantasia. Big Tech pushing out AI as fast as it can? Wile E Coyote sawing through the branch he’s sitting on. AI investment market? Any of Caine’s quests in the Amazing Digital Circus. We’re all along for the ride, whether we like it or not. ®

item.title: AI inference is running into a memory bottleneck. Huawei wants to tackle it with OceanStor M900
item.description: As organizations move from straightforward AI interactions towards longer conversations, complex reasoning and autonomous agents, the demands on their infrastructure are changing. Processing increasingly large amounts of context places significant pressure on memory capacity, while keeping accelerators supplied with data becomes just as important as raw computing power. One particular challenge is the key-value (KV) cache, which stores information generated during inference so models can reuse previous computations rather than repeatedly processing the same context. As context windows expand and multi-turn interactions become more demanding, these caches grow considerably. GPU memory and system memory provide fast access but are expensive and capacity constrained. Traditional storage offers greater capacity, yet its longer, CPU-mediated data paths can introduce latency that leaves valuable accelerator resources waiting for data. Huawei believes addressing this gap requires a different approach to storage. Bringing context memory closer to compute At HUAWEI CONNECT 2026 in Shanghai, Huawei introduced OceanStor M900 Context Memory Storage, designed to support AI inference across hyperscale datacenters and its Ascend SuperPoD infrastructure. The platform introduces what Huawei describes as a dedicated Context Memory Storage layer, extending KV cache beyond accelerator and system memory into a shared, multi-tier storage pool. Using Huawei's UnifiedBus high-speed interconnect, OceanStor M900 enables KV cache resources to be shared across a cluster, with Huawei claiming capacity of up to 64PB and substantially more context available per NPU. Its innovative ASU disk also integrates CPU, networking and storage controller functions. Combined with native KV semantics, this allows NPUs to access stored cache data in a single hop, avoiding conventional protocol conversion and CPU forwarding. According to Huawei, this approach reduces access latency to 60 microseconds, potentially doubling token throughput and halving time to first token in typical AI coding workloads. Cost and durability are also part of the proposition. Huawei's KV-aware adaptive storage technology manages data placement according to cache lifecycles, with claimed endurance of up to 24 drive writes per day, or 16 times that of conventional SSDs. The company argues this could reduce replacement and maintenance costs over time. The wider significance of OceanStor M900 lies in Huawei's approach to AI infrastructure. Rather than treating storage as a separate supporting component, the company is positioning memory, networking and compute as increasingly interconnected elements of inference performance. As agentic AI workloads grow, how efficiently infrastructure retains, shares and retrieves context may become as important as how quickly its accelerators can process it. Sponsored by Huawei

The company argues this could reduce replacement and maintenance costs over time. The wider significance of OceanStor M900 lies in Huawei's approach to AI infrastructure. Rather than treating storage as a separate supporting component, the company is positioning memory, networking and compute as increasingly interconnected elements of inference performance. As agentic AI workloads grow, how efficiently infrastructure retains, shares and retrieves context may become as important as how quickly its accelerators can process it. Sponsored by Huawei

item.description: Getting rid of head coach is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something different At the final whistle at Elland Road the TV cameras cut to a lingering shot of the Manchester United chief executive, Omar Berrada, looking down pensively from the stands, deciding, it is to be hoped, on a little clemency, a re-sheathing of the managerial shotgun. Here we have the man who hired the man. The man who fires the man. The man who also hired or rehired the previous two men he had to fire. Berrada was poached from Manchester City on the basis of his ability to grow commercial revenue (yes, OK, stop laughing), and appears, like everyone else with any actual reach around here, to exist in a strangely consequence-free bubble. item.title: Returning the first samples from a Martian moon: Inside the science of Japan's bold MMX mission to Mars
item.description: null Editor's note: Japan launched its bold MMX sample-return mission to the Mars moon Phobos on Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT). Watch a replay of the liftoff and read our launch story here. Japan's mission to Mars is one of the most ambitious in spaceflight history. It aims to become the first spacecraft to return to Earth from Mars orbit, carrying with it the first-ever samples from the Red Planet system. The mission, known as Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), is a first-of-its-kind endeavor to study the origin of Mars' moons Phobos and Deimos. The robust undertaking includes a landing on Phobos to collect the samples — which will likely be the first from the Mars system to return to Earth — and a search for evidence that could shed light on events during the formation of the solar system billions of years ago. MMX launched on an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center on Monday (Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan, Oct. 20). After a 10-month journey to reach Mars, the spacecraft will spend about three years studying Phobos, deploying a rover and landing to collect its samples. The mission will then shift its focus to Deimos for a series of flybys before departing for Earth in November 2030. If all goes according to plan, the MMX sample-return capsule is scheduled to land in Australia in 2031. The spacecraft The MMX spacecraft is comprised of three main parts, as well as a small rover. After release from its H3 launch vehicle, a propulsion module will provide the boost to put MMX on course for Mars. MMX's main exploration module carries the microwave-size IDEFIX rover and most of the mission's scientific instruments, while the return module houses the sample-return capsule. Japan's Mitsubishi Electric built MMX's three main modules, with the French space agency CNES (Centre National d'Études Spatiales) and Germany's DLR (Deutsches Zentrum für Luft-und Raumfahrt) jointly developing IDEFIX . The little rover is named for a dog in the 1960s French comic "Asterix," in a nod to the country's first satellite , Astérix, which launched in 1965. IDEFIX carries a suite of cameras, as well as the Raman Spectrometer for MMX (RAX) and miniaturized radiometer (miniRAD) instruments to analyze Phobos' surface composition and temperature. The Propulsion Module (left) and Exploration and Return Modules (right), which together make up Japan’s Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft, are seen at the Tanegashima Space Center in Minamitane, Kagoshima prefecture on Aug. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Yuichi YAMAZAKI / AFP via Getty Images)) Most of MMX's scientific instruments are housed on the exploration module, like NASA's Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE, pronounced "meh-gah-nay") device, a gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL), and France's MIRS (MMX InfraRed Spectrometer) instrument. item.dc:creator: Josh Dinner
item.content:encoded: null Editor's note: Japan launched its bold MMX sample-return mission to the Mars moon Phobos on Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT). Watch a replay of the liftoff and read our launch story here. Japan's mission to Mars is one of the most ambitious in spaceflight history. It aims to become the first spacecraft to return to Earth from Mars orbit, carrying with it the first-ever samples from the Red Planet system. The mission, known as Martian Moons eXploration (MMX), is a first-of-its-kind endeavor to study the origin of Mars' moons Phobos and Deimos. The robust undertaking includes a landing on Phobos to collect the samples — which will likely be the first from the Mars system to return to Earth — and a search for evidence that could shed light on events during the formation of the solar system billions of years ago. MMX launched on an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center on Monday (Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan, Oct. 20). After a 10-month journey to reach Mars, the spacecraft will spend about three years studying Phobos, deploying a rover and landing to collect its samples. The mission will then shift its focus to Deimos for a series of flybys before departing for Earth in November 2030. If all goes according to plan, the MMX sample-return capsule is scheduled to land in Australia in 2031. The spacecraft The MMX spacecraft is comprised of three main parts, as well as a small rover. After release from its H3 launch vehicle, a propulsion module will provide the boost to put MMX on course for Mars. MMX's main exploration module carries the microwave-size IDEFIX rover and most of the mission's scientific instruments, while the return module houses the sample-return capsule. Japan's Mitsubishi Electric built MMX's three main modules, with the French space agency CNES (Centre National d'Études Spatiales) and Germany's DLR (Deutsches Zentrum für Luft-und Raumfahrt) jointly developing IDEFIX . The little rover is named for a dog in the 1960s French comic "Asterix," in a nod to the country's first satellite , Astérix, which launched in 1965. IDEFIX carries a suite of cameras, as well as the Raman Spectrometer for MMX (RAX) and miniaturized radiometer (miniRAD) instruments to analyze Phobos' surface composition and temperature. The Propulsion Module (left) and Exploration and Return Modules (right), which together make up Japan’s Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft, are seen at the Tanegashima Space Center in Minamitane, Kagoshima prefecture on Aug. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Yuichi YAMAZAKI / AFP via Getty Images)) Most of MMX's scientific instruments are housed on the exploration module, like NASA's Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE, pronounced "meh-gah-nay") device, a gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL), and France's MIRS (MMX InfraRed Spectrometer) instrument. The exploration module also houses the Japanese-built TENGOO (TElescopic Nadir imager for GeOmOrphology) tight-zoom camera, wide-angle OROCHI (Optical RadiOmeter composed of CHromatic Imagers) multispectral camera, laser altimeter (LIDAR) and Mass Spectrum Analyzer (MSA). The return module, meanwhile, carries Japan's Circum-Martian Dust Monitor (CMDM) and Interplanetary Radiation Environment Monitor (IREM). The mission MMX will arrive in orbit around Mars in August 2027, at which point it will shed its propulsion module and transition into a quasi-satellite orbit (QSO) around Phobos that allows the probe to fly in a sort of formation with the small, asteroid -sized moon as they both circle the Red Planet. The spacecraft will spend its first few months in the Martian system observing Phobos from different altitudes, using its TENGOO and OROCHI cameras, LIDAR and MSA to map the moon's surface, study its composition and select potential landing sites. IDEFIX will be released in late 2028 or early 2029, during the first of two MMX landing rehearsals, at about 130 feet (40 meters) above Phobos. Due to the 14-mile-wide (22 kilometers) moon's extremely low gravity , the rover will be able free-fall to the surface damage-free (hopefully), right itself after a few bounces and begin exploring to gather data on the terrain and surface conditions. An artists render of IDEFIX on the surface of Phobos. (Image credit: CNES/DLR/JAXA (ASTERIX® OBELIX® IDEFIX® © Année LES EDITIONS ALBERT RENE / GOSCINNY-UDERZO)) MMX sample collection could begin as early as December 2028, the acting director of NASA's Planetary Science Division, Lindsay Hays, said during a mission briefing on Oct. 15. The spacecraft will attempt two collection landings, with its exploration and return modules descending and returning to orbit as one vehicle. On Phobos' surface, two different sampling mechanisms — the Corer Sampling Mechanism (C-sampler) and Pneumatic Sampling Mechanism (P-sampler) — will extract and collect at least 10 grams (0.35 ounces) of material for stowage inside the spacecraft's return capsule before MMX lifts off again for orbit. After its first touchdown and sample collection, MMX will return to QSO near Phobos before descending to a second landing site for a similar attempt and subsequent return to orbit. An artist’s concept of JAXA’s MMX spacecraft during its Mars’ orbit insertion. (Image credit: JAXA) MMX will end its observations of Phobos after about three years focused on the Martian moon, and will transition into a higher, resonant orbit around Mars in 2030. That course will repeatedly intersect Deimos' path for a series of flybys to collect and compare data with those from Phobos observations as scientists aim to investigate the moons' origins. Near the end of 2030, the exploration module will separate, leaving the return module to fire its engine out of Mars' gravitational influence and begin an eight-month journey back to Earth with the collected samples. As MMX closes the last stretch of void during its approach to Earth in 2031, the sample-return capsule will separate and enter the atmosphere for a targeted parachute landing in Australia's Woomera region, where its contents will be recovered for laboratory analysis by Japan and its mission partners. Phobos and Deimos Those samples, and the data collected by MMX, could tell scientists a lot — about the moons' composition, geography and, perhaps most importantly, how they came to exist in the first place. There are two leading theories for Phobos and Deimos' origins , both of which point to very different versions of ancient Martian history. "Phobos and Deimos are interesting, but not just in their own right. Their presence is a key piece of the larger story of the Mars system," said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and scientist in NASA's Planetary Science Division, during the Oct. 15 mission briefing. "By uncovering the moons' origin, we'll gain new insights into the history of both Mars and Earth, especially those events that shaped both planets billions of years ago and helped create the worlds we see today." Both Phobos and Deimos are relatively small and irregularly shaped, and bear several resemblances and spectral characteristics to primitive D-type asteroids — ancient bodies thought to preserve material dating back to the solar system's formation about 4.6 billion years ago. Those similarities suggest Phobos and Deimos may have formed elsewhere in the solar system and were later captured by Mars' gravity. Phobos is the larger of Mars' two small moons and bears the scars of millennia of small impacts. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona) Their near-circular, equatorially-aligned orbits around the Red Planet, however, somewhat complicate that theory. For example, a captured asteroid would be much more likely to have entered an elongated and tilted orbit akin to the direction and velocity of its original approach, scientists say. item.title: Computer scientist Margaret Hamilton was a problem-solver for the ages (op-ed)
item.description: null Dean Robbins is a journalist and children's author. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights . The pioneering computer scientist Margaret Hamilton , who died on Sept. 30 at age 90, played a key role in putting astronauts on the moon. She was a problem-solver extraordinaire, and it all started in early childhood. Considering the name "daddy longlegs" unfair to female arachnids, young Margaret decided to call half of them "mommy longlegs." Wondering why the neighborhood baseball players were all boys, she determined to join the team herself. As she grew up in the 1940s and '50s, Margaret noticed a similar problem with various professions. Why were doctors, judges and scientists almost always men? The solution: she would study hard in school and prepare herself for any job she might care to do. It's no surprise that a born problem-solver would gravitate to computers. In the late 1950s, the new technology offered mind-bending possibilities, and this college math major saw a chance to put her skills to use on a cosmic scale. Hamilton had long been a stargazer, thanks to a philosophical father who taught her to love the night sky . In 1965, after stints in meteorology and satellite tracking, she became interested in a Massachusetts Institute of Technology project that designed in-flight computers for NASA's moon mission. The team, of course, consisted solely of men. But, just as with her neighborhood baseball team, Hamilton refused to accept limitations for herself or anybody else. She kicked open the door and quickly rose to director of software engineering. With her knack for devising novel solutions to seemingly insoluble problems, no one was better suited for the job. Working with the era's primitive technology, Margaret thought through the various mishaps that could occur on a spaceflight and designed the software to handle every contingency. The epochal Apollo 11 moon mission of 1969 put her planning to the test. As astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin neared the moon's surface in their lunar module, an error overloaded the onboard computer's processing unit. Mission Control faced the prospect of aborting the landing, but Margaret's ingenious programming allowed the system to prioritize essential tasks while canceling the inessential ones. The lunar module touched down without a hitch, and Armstrong and Aldrin became famous. An excerpt from Dean Robbins' 2017 book "Margaret and the Moon: How Margaret Hamilton Saved the First Lunar Landing." Used by permission of Alfred A. Knopf, an imprint of Random House Children's Books, a division of Penguin Random House LLC. All rights reserved.) Sadly, Margaret Hamilton did not.
